13 · Q4 Pulse 3: how the conversations unfolded

Opening request → 2nd message → when they shared background information

Denicia Aragon Espinosa

November 09, 2026

In short

  • All 52 chats were followed past the first message. 1 chat (a pasted email draft with no health request) is left out of the charts and counts below, so they use 51 chats (your decision L28). The paths were coded with the frozen path codebook (path_frozen_2026-11-05_v1; later updated to v2 and v3, see What the coders said about the codebook and Update: implied requests).
  • 20 chats (39%) stopped after one message. The other 32 were coded by 3 independent AI coders.
  • After the first message, the most common next step was “Shared more about themselves” (18 chats, 35%).
  • Of the 22 chats where column 3 applies, background information came with the first message in 8, after the AI asked in 8, and never in 6. Nobody shared background information on their own later (0 chats), so that box is left out of the charts.
  • The coders agreed closely: all 3 gave the same column-2 label for 100.0% of chats and the same column-3 label for 96.9% (κ = 1.0 and 0.97).
  • 144 of 144 evidence quotes were found word for word in the chats. 0 chat(s) were flagged for your review.

What we did, step by step

  1. Froze the codebook. After you approved the 9 pilot edits, the path codebook was locked in a dated folder (path_frozen_2026-11-05_v1). Each file has a fingerprint (a hash). The fingerprints were checked again just before coding, so we know the coders used exactly this text.
  2. Column 1 was not coded again. It comes straight from the final step-10 request types, grouped as you decided: Asking to understand (R1, R2, R7), Asking what to do (R3, R5, R6) and Just sharing information (R4 only). If a chat had both, action wins. Since request codebook v6 (decision L27), a bare symptom or an own pasted result counts as an implied request, so Just sharing information now holds only chats with no health request at all. The only chat left in Just sharing information was an email draft with no health request; you decided to leave it out of the charts (L28), so the charts show 2 opening groups and use 51 chats.
  3. Chats that stopped. If there is no real participant message after the first one (a “thanks” alone does not count), the chat is Stopped after one message. The computer found these 20 chats; they were not sent to the coders.
  4. 3 independent coders. Each of the other 32 chats was coded by 3 fresh AI coders. Each saw the chats in its own shuffled order (fixed seeds 13101, 13102, 13103). None of them saw the draft or pilot labels. For every label they had to copy an exact quote as evidence.
  5. Final label = majority. A label is final when at least 2 of the 3 coders chose it. Anything without a majority is flagged for you rather than decided by the computer.

The flow chart

Each dark bar is a group of chats (in the middle column, the pale box next to it holds its label); the bands show how chats moved from one column to the next. Band colours follow the opening request. Percentages are of the 51 chats in the charts.

cols <- c("Asking to understand" = "#29ABE2", "Asking what to do" = "#1E6FA8",
          "Just sharing information" = "#7FC7E8")
nd <- nodes |> mutate(across(c(x0, x1, x_lane, ymin, ymax, n, pct), num), column = num(column),
                      ymid = (ymin + ymax) / 2,
                      lab = ifelse(column == 2, stringr::str_wrap(label, 21), label),
                      text = paste0(lab, "\n", pct(pct), " (n = ", n, ")"),
                      lines = stringr::str_count(text, "\n") + 1,
                      tx = ifelse(column == 1, x0 - 0.03, x1 + 0.025),
                      hj = ifelse(column == 1, 1, 0))
# Keep labels in the same column from touching: move a label down only if it would overlap the one above.
line_h <- 2.3
nd <- nd |> group_by(column) |> arrange(desc(ymid), .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(ylab = purrr::accumulate2(ymid[-1], (lines[-1] + head(lines, -1)) / 2 * line_h + 0.8,
                                   function(prev, y, sep) min(y, prev - sep), .init = ymid[1]) |> unlist()) |>
  ungroup()
pl <- polys |> mutate(across(c(x, y, point), num)) |> arrange(link_id, point)
heads <- tibble(x = c(0, 1 + (0.07 + 0.78) / 2, max(nd$x0)) + c(0.035, 0, 0.035), y = 3.5,
                lab = c("Opening request", "2nd message", "When they shared\nbackground information"))

p_flow <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = pl, aes(x, y, group = link_id, fill = group), alpha = 0.6, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_rect(data = filter(nd, column == 2), aes(xmin = x1, xmax = x_lane, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), fill = "#DCEAF5") +
  geom_rect(data = nd, aes(xmin = x0, xmax = x1, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), fill = "#0A2440") +
  geom_label(data = nd, aes(tx, ylab, label = text, hjust = hj), size = 5.6, lineheight = 0.95,
             label.size = 0, fill = alpha("white", 0.9), colour = "#0A2440", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(data = heads, aes(x, y, label = lab), size = 7, fontface = "bold", colour = "#0A2440",
            vjust = 0, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = "Opening request") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.7, 3.75)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(min(c(nd$ymin, nd$ylab - 4)) - 1, 9)) +
  labs(title = path_title,
       subtitle = path_subtitle,
       caption = paste0(path_caption, "\nBand thickness = number of chats.")) +
  theme_void(base_size = 20) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 18),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 26, colour = "#0A2440"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 19, colour = "#164E7C", margin = margin(4, 0, 10, 0)),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 15, colour = "#3A4B5B", hjust = 0, margin = margin(10, 0, 0, 0)),
        plot.title.position = "plot", plot.caption.position = "plot",
        plot.margin = margin(14, 14, 10, 14))
save_fig("13_chat_paths_flow.png", p_flow, width = 16, height = 12.8)
p_flow

There is also an interactive version, 13_chat_paths_flow_interactive.html (open it in a browser and hover over a band to see its number of chats).

Left out: On their own later has 0 chats, so it is not drawn. Nobody shared background information on their own; it is still defined in the codebook.

How to read it. Column 3 only applies to chats whose 2nd message asked what to do or shared more about themselves, so it is shorter than the other columns. Chats in the other column-2 groups stop at column 2.

What we mean by “background information”

tibble(Term = c("Background information", "With the first message", "After the AI asked", "Never shared",
                "On their own later"),
       `What it means` = c(
         paste("Facts about the person or their situation that give the AI context: age, weight or height,",
               "health history and other conditions, medicines, how long the problem has lasted, other symptoms",
               "beyond the main problem, habits or activity level, and recent events or care that led up to the problem.",
               "It does NOT include the main complaint itself (for example \"my foot hurts\"), more description of",
               "the main problem, or \"what if\" symptoms."),
         "Background information was already in the first message we coded.",
         paste("They shared background information after the AI asked a question, or invited it",
               "(for example \"If you tell me X, I can\u2026\")."),
         "They never shared any background information in the chat.",
         "They shared it later without being asked. No chat did this (0 chats), so it is not shown in the charts.")) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"), locations = cells_body(columns = Term)) |>
  cols_width(Term ~ px(230))
Term What it means
Background information Facts about the person or their situation that give the AI context: age, weight or height, health history and other conditions, medicines, how long the problem has lasted, other symptoms beyond the main problem, habits or activity level, and recent events or care that led up to the problem. It does NOT include the main complaint itself (for example "my foot hurts"), more description of the main problem, or "what if" symptoms.
With the first message Background information was already in the first message we coded.
After the AI asked They shared background information after the AI asked a question, or invited it (for example "If you tell me X, I can…").
Never shared They never shared any background information in the chat.
On their own later They shared it later without being asked. No chat did this (0 chats), so it is not shown in the charts.

The tree view

The same results as a tree, read from top to bottom: the opening request, then what the 2nd message did, then (under Then asked what to do and Shared more about themselves) when background information was shared. Thicker lines mean more chats. Every % is out of the 51 chats in the charts. It works like a decision tree: the 3 opening requests sit side by side across the top, and each one has its own branches underneath (so labels repeat across the 3 groups). Under each opening request, the boxes are in order from most to fewest chats, and the thicker line goes to the largest branch. Under Then asked what to do and Shared more about themselves, a third level shows when background information was shared. Empty boxes are left out.

source(here::here("scripts", "13_code-chat-paths", "13d_tree_chart.R"))
lay <- tree_layout(final, n_all)
p_tree <- tree_chart(lay) +
  labs(title = path_title, subtitle = path_subtitle,
       caption = paste0(path_caption, "\nThicker line = the largest branch under each box. Empty boxes are left out."))
save_fig("13_chat_paths_tree.png", p_tree, width = 14, height = 10)
p_tree

The numbers, with 95% confidence intervals

We only have 51 chats, so each % is an estimate. The 95% confidence interval is the range where the “true” % for people like these probably lies. When two ranges overlap a lot, do not read much into the difference. (They are Wilson intervals, which work well for small samples.) On their own later (0 chats) is left out of the table.

counts |>
  filter(num(n) > 0) |>
  mutate(Chats = num(n), `% of chats` = pct(pct),
         `95% confidence interval` = paste0(pct(ci_low), " to ", pct(ci_high)),
         `% of chats where column 3 applies` = ifelse(is.na(pct_of_col3_base), "",
                                                      paste0(pct(pct_of_col3_base), " of ", base_col3))) |>
  select(column, Label = label, Chats, `% of chats`, `95% confidence interval`, `% of chats where column 3 applies`) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "column") |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"), locations = cells_row_groups())

How well the coders agreed

Percent agreement is the share of chats where all 3 coders gave the same answer. κ (kappa) also allows for agreement that could happen by chance (1 = perfect, 0 = no better than chance). κ shows how consistently the coders applied the codebook; it does not prove the labels are right. With 32 chats, and small groups, κ is a rough guide; for rare codes it can jump around.

agree |>
  mutate(fleiss_kappa = ifelse(is.na(fleiss_kappa) | fleiss_kappa == "", "–", fleiss_kappa)) |>
  select(`What was coded` = what, Chats = chats_coded, `All 3 agree` = all_3_agree,
         `% all 3 agree` = pct_all_3, `At least 2 agree` = at_least_2_agree, `κ` = fleiss_kappa) |>
  gt()
What was coded Chats All 3 agree % all 3 agree At least 2 agree κ
Which turn is the 2nd message 32 32 100.0 32 <U+2013>
Column 2: 2nd message 32 32 100.0 32 1.0
Column 3: background information (empty = not coded) 32 31 96.9 32 0.97
Turn where background was first shared 32 32 100.0 32 <U+2013>

What the coders said about the codebook

The open point, and your decision (analyst, 2026-11-05). All 3 coders raised the same question on their own: when the AI ends with an invitation such as “If you tell me where the pain is, I can …”, does that count as the AI asked? You first answered no (log L25), then changed your mind (log L26): “that should be considered ‘ai asked’ because they were primed to give that information”. So an invitation now counts as After the AI asked.

  • The codebook wording changed, so a new dated freeze was made (path_frozen_2026-11-05_v2) and v1 was marked as superseded. Both stay locked; v1 is the version the coders used.
  • The 2 chats where this happened (66d9e5be and 69fff128) were recoded by the analyst from On their own later to After the AI asked. They were the only On their own later chats, and both followed an invitation, so no other chat was affected.
  • The coders’ own labels are kept in the workbook (col3_coders) next to the final label.

Update: implied requests (column 1, decision L27, 2026-11-09)

You checked the Just sharing information group and found that some of those chats did ask something: either later in the message, without a question mark, or simply by describing a symptom. You decided:

  • Request wording anywhere in the first message counts, with or without a “?”.
  • A bare symptom or health change of your own counts as an implied “Why is this happening to me?” (R1), and a pasted result of your own counts as an implied “Explain my test results” (R7).

What we did. The request codebook was re-frozen as v6 (step 09), and 3 new independent AI coders recoded the 9 Just sharing chats with the new rule (they agreed on every chat, ? = 1.0; see step 10). Column 1 was then rebuilt from the new step-10 labels, and the path codebook was re-frozen as path_frozen_2026-11-09_v3. Columns 2 and 3 did not change.

What else the coders said

The coders also mentioned that short time words (“lately”, “started yesterday”) and the stressors in mental-health chats were hard to place. These did not change any final label.

feedback |> mutate(feedback = mask_names(feedback)) |> select(Coder = coder, Feedback = feedback) |> gt()
Coder Feedback
1 D2 close call vs D3 examples: the D2 rule says unrequested background after any AI question counts as D2, but the D3 examples (69fff128, 66d9e5be) follow AI turns ending in a conditional request ('If you tell me where the pain is...'); the codebook should say whether such conditional requests count as 'the AI asked'. Short overall durations like 'started hurting yesterday' (69600cc8) or vague 'lately' (63e55f08) are hard to place between background duration and main complaint. In mental-health chats (6a0206ae) the line between main complaint and background is unclear. Fragmentary first messages (6a10664c 'I get this time time') are hard to judge for D1.
2 The 'AI asked' rule does not say whether 'If you tell me X, I can...' offers count as a question; this decided D2 vs D3 in 66d9e5be and 69fff128, whose messages the codebook itself lists as D3 examples although the AI had just invited more detail. Very short onset statements ('started hurting yesterday', 69600cc8) and vague 'lately' (63e55f08) are not clearly covered by the overall-duration rule. Named conditions that are the main complaint (eczema in 6acb95ac) could be read as health history. Implied questions such as 'I don't know if that means anything' (66d8e4c1) sit between M3 and M1. Whether causes/situations in mental-health chats (stressors in 6a0206ae) are main problem or background is unclear.
3 D2 close call ('AI asked but person shares a different, unrequested piece of background still counts as D2') conflicts with the D3 examples: in 69fff128 and 66d9e5be the AI turn just before ended with 'If you tell me where the pain is...', yet the codebook uses these exact replies as D3 examples. Unclear whether 'If you tell me X, I can...' counts as a real AI question. Vague timing words ('lately' in 63e55f08, 'I get this time time' in 6a10664c, 'started yesterday' in 69600cc8) are not clearly covered by the overall-duration rule. 'What if I am spitting blood' (671a8337) may be a real new symptom phrased as a what-if; the codebook does not say how to tell. For mental-health chats (6a0206ae) it is unclear whether stressors are the main complaint or background.
